flow_transcript_slices.candidate_transcript:
[Q1 Attempt 1]
So, I am, I just moved back to California about a year ago. I've been working in education for a little while. So, I started off working as a substitute for a school district in Rosemont, and then gradually I, you know, got into the daycare centers. So, I've worked with pretty much all ages, mostly two- to five-year-olds. I'm just really passionate about working in the education field. I also have two kids of my own, so I know that early childhood education is, like, super important. Like, the development stages between zero and five were the most crucial. So, I just love being a part of that, getting to know. You know, the kids in the community and, you know, just helping them grow and develop. And then education, I do have my bachelor's degree. flow_transcript_slices.question: Tell me about a time a child was having a really hard moment emotionally. What did you notice about what they were feeling, and how did you respond?
flow_transcript_slices.candidate_transcript:
[Q3 Attempt 1]
So I've had plenty of cases like that, especially working in the four and five-year-old classrooms. There's a lot of emotions there. Usually I try to take them aside and give them time to talk about how they're feeling and then just kind of motivate them to think more positively, like redirect them and then just create that positive environment for them. And, you know, like they just, they really want to know that you're paying attention to them, you're hearing them and their feelings.

um so one of the classrooms i went in was a little more chaotic the there wasn't a lot of structure um so you know kids were running a mock and um so it did create a little bit of um stress but uh one of the things that i've learned over the years working with children is you have to be patient um and so uh basically it's just um i don't know it's all about your your mindset right so if you're overwhelmed they're gonna feel overwhelmed so um i always you know kind of implement the same um the same um what's the word like skills uh habits to do myself so for instance if you're trying to say let's take 10 breaths and calm down kind of do that that same technique for myself so that um i was in a good mindset for the kids

flow_transcript_slices.question: Imagine you’re caring for a child who clearly does not want to be touched during a routine task, like diapering, helping with clothing, or guiding them physically. They are pulling away or saying no. Walk me through exactly what you would do, step by step
flow_transcript_slices.candidate_transcript:
[Q5 Attempt 1]
Um, so I, I would say it's important to get, make sure they, um, are given their space. You never want to, you know, tug on a child accidentally with them. Um, you kind of just want to like get down on their level and, um, like I said, redirection or, um, instead of, uh, continuously telling them, Hey, um, you know, this is what we're going to do. You can give them like two choices, like, Hey, um, first we're going to do this and then we're going to do this. So, um, first we're going to use the bathroom and then we're going to do, um, Play-Doh for example. So, um, kind of giving them that direction and then something positive afterwards so that they know, Hey, if I do this and I do a good job, I'm going to earn this.
